draft.title: Making proteins
card: A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a polypeptide, which folds to make a protein. Making it takes two stages.
the DNA of a gene is copied into a strand of mRNA. In eukaryotic cells this happens in the nucleus, and the mRNA then moves out to the cytoplasm.
a ribosome reads the mRNA in codons, which are groups of three bases. Each codon calls for one amino acid.
tRNA molecules carry amino acids to the ribosome. Each tRNA matches a codon and brings its amino acid, and the amino acids join in order to build the polypeptide.
draft.remember: Transcription copies a gene into mRNA. Translation reads the mRNA to build a polypeptide.

a.q: Which process builds a polypeptide by reading mRNA codons at a ribosome?
opts: Translation
Transcription
Replication
Crossing over
a.why: Translation is the stage where a ribosome reads the mRNA codons and tRNA brings the matching amino acids. Transcription is tempting, but it only copies the gene's DNA into mRNA and does not build the polypeptide.
a.clue: Which stage uses ribosomes and amino acids?

b.q: In a liver cell, a gene is switched on and its mRNA is made. Which statement describes what happens next to that mRNA?
opts: A ribosome reads it in codons and tRNA brings amino acids
tRNA copies it into a new strand of DNA in the nucleus
A ribosome copies it into a second strand of mRNA
Each base is read singly and calls for one amino acid
b.why: After transcription, the mRNA is read by a ribosome in codons, and tRNA brings the matching amino acids to build a polypeptide. Reading single bases is wrong because a codon is a group of three bases, and each codon calls for one amino acid.
b.clue: Think about the size of the group of bases that is read.

b.best: A ribosome reads it in codons and tRNA brings amino acids

problems.detail: "Each codon calls for one amino acid" is not true of stop codons, which code for no amino acid and end translation. Year 12 students meet start and stop codons, so this needs a qualifier, e.g. "Most codons call for one amino acid; stop codons end the chain."
The why repeats the overstatement that each codon calls for one amino acid, which ignores stop codons.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The card and why (b) say every codon calls for an amino acid, which is false for stop codons and should be qualified.
